findings.description: The EC2 instance's user_data script contains hardcoded AWS access key ID and secret access key (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY). These credentials are stored in Terraform state, readable from instance metadata, and exposed to anyone with console or API access to the instance.
The security group opens TCP port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing SSH brute-force and exploitation attempts from anywhere on the internet.
The security group allows TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the web service to the entire internet (acceptable for public web content, but broad and worth confirming).
The S3 bucket used for VPC flow logs has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so flow log data is stored unencrypted at rest.
The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, and force_destroy is enabled, so the bucket can be made public and its contents deleted; flow logs could be exposed or destroyed by an attacker.
map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so every instance launched into this subnet receives a public IP, increasing attack surface for any workloads placed there.
map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so instances launched into this subnet automatically receive public IP addresses.
The EBS volume attached to the portal server has no encrypted = true setting, so its data is stored unencrypted and could be read if the volume or snapshot is compromised.
The snapshot of the portal disk is unencrypted, so the disk contents including any secrets on it are exposed at rest in the snapshot.
The security group permits all outbound traffic (protocol -1, 0.0.0.0/0), which enables unrestricted data exfiltration from a compromised instance.
The route table routes 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway and is associated with both subnets, making them publicly routable and reachable from the internet when combined with public IPs.
